claim: Cancer stem cells (CSCs) undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to drive metastatic dissemination in experimental cancer models.
source: Cancer stem cells (CSCs) undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to drive metastatic dissemination in experimental cancer models.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Biddle et al., 2011; Lawson et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2014; Ruscetti et al., 2016) as indicated in the full manuscript text.

claim: Tumour cells undergoing EMT have not been observed disseminating into the tissue surrounding human tumour specimens.
source: However, tumour cells undergoing EMT have not been observed disseminating into the tissue surrounding human tumour specimens, leaving the relevance to human cancer uncertain.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior observations in the literature, establishing the knowledge gap.

claim: EpCAM and CD24 have been previously identified as CSC markers that, alongside Vimentin, identify EMT CSCs in human oral cancer cell lines.
source: We have previously identified both EpCAM and CD24 as CSC markers that, alongside the mesenchymal marker Vimentin, identify EMT CSCs in human oral cancer cell lines.
evidence: Refers to prior work by the authors establishing these markers.

claim: There is a significant enrichment of EpCAM, CD24 and Vimentin co-stained cells disseminating beyond the tumour body in metastatic specimens.
source: Examining disseminating tumour cells in over 12,000 imaging fields from 74 human oral tumours, we see a significant enrichment of EpCAM, CD24 and Vimentin co-stained cells disseminating beyond the tumour body in metastatic specimens.
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of imaging data from 74 tumours.

claim: An artificial neural network trained on EpCAM, CD24, and Vimentin staining predicts metastasis with cross-validated accuracy of 87–89%.
source: Through training an artificial neural network, these predict metastasis with high accuracy (cross-validated accuracy of 87–89%).
evidence: Supported by machine learning analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Single disseminating EMT CSCs have been observed in human oral cancer specimens.
source: In this study, we have observed single disseminating EMT CSCs in human oral cancer specimens, and these are highly predictive of metastatic disease.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescent imaging data showing individual cells.

claim: Disseminating EMT CSCs are highly predictive of metastatic disease.
source: In this study, we have observed single disseminating EMT CSCs in human oral cancer specimens, and these are highly predictive of metastatic disease.
evidence: Supported by machine learning prediction results correlating these cells with metastasis.

claim: In multiple types of carcinoma, cancer stem cells (CSCs) undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to enable metastatic dissemination from the primary tumour.
source: In multiple types of carcinoma, cancer stem cells (CSCs) undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to enable metastatic dissemination from the primary tumour (Biddle et al., 2011; Lawson et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2014; Ruscetti et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: The model of metastatic dissemination via EMT has been built from studies using murine models and human cancer cell line models.
source: This model of metastatic dissemination has been built from studies using murine models and human cancer cell line models.
evidence: Statement about the basis of current knowledge in the field.

claim: The EMT process has not been observed in human tumours in the in vivo setting, leading to uncertainty over the relevance of these findings to human tumour metastasis.
source: However, this process has not been observed in human tumours in the in vivo setting, leading to uncertainty over the relevance of these findings to human tumour metastasis (Bill and Christofori, 2015; Williams et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations discussing the knowledge gap.

claim: A key complication with efforts to study metastatic processes in human tumours is the inability to trace cell lineage.
source: A key complication with efforts to study metastatic processes in human tumours is the inability to trace cell lineage.
evidence: Statement about a methodological challenge in the field.

claim: Cancer cells exiting the tumour downregulate epithelial markers whilst undergoing EMT, making them indistinguishable from mesenchymal non-tumour cells surrounding the tumour.
source: As cancer cells exiting the tumour downregulate epithelial markers whilst undergoing EMT, they become indistinguishable from the mesenchymal non-tumour cells surrounding the tumour (Li and Kang, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Once cancer cells detach from the tumour body and move away they are lost to analysis.
source: Therefore, once these cells detach from the tumour body and move away they are lost to analysis.
evidence: Logical inference from the previous statement about marker downregulation.

claim: Attempts have been made to use the retention of epithelial markers alongside acquisition of mesenchymal markers to identify cells undergoing EMT in human tumours.
source: Attempts have been made to use the retention of epithelial markers alongside acquisition of mesenchymal markers to identify cells undergoing EMT in human tumours (Bronsert et al., 2014; Jensen et al., 2015; Puram et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Previous studies using epithelial and mesenchymal markers were limited to characterising cells undergoing the earliest stages of EMT whilst still attached to the cohesive body of the primary tumour.
source: However, these studies were limited to characterising cells undergoing the earliest stages of EMT whilst still attached to the cohesive body of the primary tumour.
evidence: Critical assessment of prior work based on their methodological limitations.

claim: EMT must be followed by the reverse process of mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET) to enable new tumour growth at secondary sites.
source: EMT must be followed by the reverse process of mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET) to enable new tumour growth at secondary sites, and therefore retained plasticity manifested as ability to revert to an epithelial phenotype is an important feature of metastatic CSCs (Ocaña et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Retained plasticity manifested as ability to revert to an epithelial phenotype is an important feature of metastatic CSCs.
source: EMT must be followed by the reverse process of mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET) to enable new tumour growth at secondary sites, and therefore retained plasticity manifested as ability to revert to an epithelial phenotype is an important feature of metastatic CSCs (Ocaña et al., 2012; Tsai et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations and logical inference from the requirement for MET.

claim: A CD44highEpCAMlow/- EMT population can be separated from the main CD44lowEpCAMhigh epithelial population in flow cytometric analysis of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) cell lines and fresh tumour specimens.
source: We have previously demonstrated that a CD44highEpCAMlow/- EMT population can be separated from the main CD44lowEpCAMhigh epithelial population in flow cytometric analysis of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) cell lines and fresh tumour specimens (Biddle et al., 2016; Biddle et al., 2011).
evidence: Refers to prior work by the authors.

claim: Retained cell surface expression of EpCAM was identified in a minority of cells that have undergone a full morphological EMT.
source: We identified retained cell surface expression of EpCAM (Biddle et al., 2011) and CD24 (Biddle et al., 2016) in a minority of cells that have undergone a full morphological EMT.
evidence: Refers to prior work by the authors.

claim: Retained cell surface expression of CD24 was identified in a minority of cells that have undergone a full morphological EMT.
source: We identified retained cell surface expression of EpCAM (Biddle et al., 2011) and CD24 (Biddle et al., 2016) in a minority of cells that have undergone a full morphological EMT.
evidence: Refers to prior work by the authors.

claim: Both EpCAM and CD24 were individually associated with enhanced ability to undergo MET.
source: Both EpCAM and CD24 were individually associated with enhanced ability to undergo MET, and thus are markers of EMT CSCs exhibiting retained plasticity.
evidence: Refers to prior findings by the authors.

claim: EpCAM and CD24 are markers of EMT CSCs exhibiting retained plasticity.
source: Both EpCAM and CD24 were individually associated with enhanced ability to undergo MET, and thus are markers of EMT CSCs exhibiting retained plasticity.
evidence: Inference from the association with MET ability.

claim: Retention of EpCAM or CD24 may identify an important population of tumour cells that have undergone EMT and disseminated from the primary tumour in human tumour specimens.
source: We therefore reasoned that retention of one or both of these markers may identify an important population of tumour cells that have undergone EMT and disseminated from the primary tumour in human tumour specimens, and are responsible for subsequent metastatic seeding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on prior findings.

claim: Tumour cells retaining EpCAM or CD24 after EMT are responsible for subsequent metastatic seeding.
source: We therefore reasoned that retention of one or both of these markers may identify an important population of tumour cells that have undergone EMT and disseminated from the primary tumour in human tumour specimens, and are responsible for subsequent metastatic seeding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that is tested in the study.

claim: Staining for EpCAM and CD24 alongside Vimentin in over 12,000 imaging fields from 74 human tumours identifies cells that have undergone EMT and disseminated into the stromal region surrounding metastatic primary tumours.
source: Staining for EpCAM and CD24 alongside the mesenchymal marker Vimentin in over 12,000 imaging fields from 74 human tumours, stratified on metastatic status, identifies cells that have undergone EMT and disseminated into the stromal region surrounding metastatic primary tumours.
evidence: Supported by the imaging data presented in the study.

claim: The presence of EMT CSCs in the tumour stroma is predictive of metastasis.
source: Using an image-based machine learning approach, we show that the presence of these EMT CSCs in the tumour stroma is predictive of metastasis.
evidence: Supported by machine learning analysis results.

claim: The retention of EpCAM expression in a sub-population of tumour cells that have undergone EMT raised the prospect that these cells may be identifiable outside of the tumour body in human tumour specimens.
source: The retention of EpCAM expression in a sub-population of tumour cells that have undergone EMT raised the prospect that we may be able to identify these cells outside of the tumour body in human tumour specimens, as EpCAM is a specific epithelial marker that would not normally be found in the surrounding stromal region.
evidence: Logical inference based on EpCAM being epithelial-specific.

claim: EpCAM is a specific epithelial marker that would not normally be found in the surrounding stromal region.
source: The retention of EpCAM expression in a sub-population of tumour cells that have undergone EMT raised the prospect that we may be able to identify these cells outside of the tumour body in human tumour specimens, as EpCAM is a specific epithelial marker that would not normally be found in the surrounding stromal region.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about EpCAM expression patterns.

claim: CD44 cannot be used as an EMT marker in the context of intact tissue as it requires trypsin degradation in order to yield differential expression in EMT and epithelial populations.
source: Notably, CD44 cannot be used as an EMT marker in the context of intact tissue as it requires trypsin degradation in order to yield differential expression in EMT and epithelial populations (Biddle et al., 2013; Mack and Gires, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Vimentin accurately distinguishes EMT from epithelial tumour cells in immunofluorescent staining protocols.
source: Vimentin, on the other hand, accurately distinguishes EMT from epithelial tumour cells in immunofluorescent staining protocols (Biddle et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ cells were greatly enriched in the EMT-stem sub-line, comprising 41% of the population, compared to 2.1% in the CA1 line.
source: EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ cells were greatly enriched in the EMT-stem sub-line, comprising 41% of the population, compared to 2.1% in the CA1 line (Figure 1A, B and E).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Cells with EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ staining profile were absent from normal keratinocyte culture and cancer associated fibroblast culture.
source: Cells with this staining profile were absent from normal keratinocyte culture and cancer associated fibroblast culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by imaging data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was very little Pan-keratin+Vim+CD24+ staining, and no enrichment for Pan-keratin+Vim+CD24+ cells in the EMT-stem sub-line.
source: There was very little Pan-keratin+Vim+CD24+ staining, and no enrichment for Pan-keratin+Vim+CD24+ cells in the EMT-stem sub-line (Figure 1C, D and E).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Whilst epithelial keratins are lost, EpCAM is retained in cells undergoing EMT.
source: Therefore, whilst epithelial keratins are lost, EpCAM is retained in cells undergoing EMT and an EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ staining profile can be used as a marker for EMT CSCs in immunofluorescent staining protocols.
evidence: Inference from the differential staining patterns observed.

claim: An EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ staining profile can be used as a marker for EMT CSCs in immunofluorescent staining protocols.
source: Therefore, whilst epithelial keratins are lost, EpCAM is retained in cells undergoing EMT and an EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ staining profile can be used as a marker for EMT CSCs in immunofluorescent staining protocols.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the cell line staining experiments.

claim: Single cells co-expressing EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 were detected in the stromal region surrounding human OSCC tumours.
source: Imaging the tumour body and adjacent stroma in sections of human OSCC specimens, we detected single cells co-expressing EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 in the stromal region surrounding the tumour (Figure 1F), confirming that these cells can be detected in human tumour specimens.
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Single cells co-expressing EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 were abundant in the stroma surrounding metastatic tumours.
source: Single cells co-expressing EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 were abundant in the stroma surrounding metastatic tumours.
evidence: Supported by imaging data from the stratified tumour cohort.

claim: Single cells co-expressing EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 were not abundant in non-metastatic tumours or normal epithelial regions.
source: This was not the case in non-metastatic tumours or normal epithelial regions (Figure 2, A-C).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Pan-keratin staining did not identify cells in the stroma surrounding metastatic tumours.
source: In contrast to EpCAM, pan-keratin staining did not identify cells in the stroma surrounding metastatic tumours (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ cells were enriched in the stroma compared to the tumour body.
source: EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ cells were enriched in the stroma compared to the tumour body, and there was a much greater accumulation of EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ cells in the stroma of metastatic tumours compared to non-metastatic tumours.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There was a much greater accumulation of EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ cells in the stroma of metastatic tumours compared to non-metastatic tumours.
source: EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ cells were enriched in the stroma compared to the tumour body, and there was a much greater accumulation of EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ cells in the stroma of metastatic tumours compared to non-metastatic tumours.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: EpCAM+Vim+CD24- cells were enriched in the stroma but showed no difference between metastatic and non-metastatic tumours.
source: Interestingly, this was not the case for EpCAM+Vim+CD24- cells, which were also enriched in the stroma but showed no difference between metastatic and non-metastatic tumours.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Pan-keratin+Vim+CD24+ cells were not detected in tumour specimens.
source: Pan-keratin+Vim+CD24+ cells were not detected.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: In a published scRNAseq dataset for human head and neck cancer, 12% of tumour cells (267/2215) were EpCAM+Vim+CD24+.
source: Analysing this dataset for EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 co-expression, we found that 12% of tumour cells (267/2215) were EpCAM+Vim+CD24+.
evidence: Analysis of published scRNAseq data from Puram et al., 2017.

claim: In a published scRNAseq dataset for human head and neck cancer, only 0.8% (29/3687) of non-tumour cells were EpCAM+Vim+CD24+.
source: In the non-tumour cells, only 0.8% (29/3687) were EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Analysis of published scRNAseq data from Puram et al., 2017.

claim: The observed EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ cells in tumour specimens are highly likely to be a tumour cell population.
source: Therefore, the observed EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ cells in our tumour specimens are highly likely to be a tumour cell population.
evidence: Inference from the scRNAseq analysis showing enrichment in tumour vs non-tumour cells.

claim: EpCAM is a specific epithelial marker that is not expressed in stromal or immune cells.
source: EpCAM is a specific epithelial marker, that is not expressed in stromal or immune cells – it is expressed exclusively in epithelia and epithelial-derived tumours (Keller et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: An EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ staining profile marks tumour cells disseminating into the surrounding stroma.
source: These findings demonstrate that an EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ staining profile marks tumour cells disseminating into the surrounding stroma, and that these cells are enriched specifically in metastatic tumours.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the imaging and quantification data.

claim: EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ cells are enriched specifically in metastatic tumours.
source: These findings demonstrate that an EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ staining profile marks tumour cells disseminating into the surrounding stroma, and that these cells are enriched specifically in metastatic tumours.
evidence: Supported by quantification data comparing metastatic and non-metastatic tumours.

claim: The presence of disseminating tumour cells that express EpCAM but not CD24 did not correlate with metastasis.
source: The presence of disseminating tumour cells that express EpCAM but not CD24 did not correlate with metastasis.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: There is a requirement for the plasticity marker CD24 when identifying disseminating metastatic CSCs.
source: This highlights a requirement for the plasticity marker CD24, when identifying disseminating metastatic CSCs.
evidence: Inference from the differential correlation with metastasis for EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ vs EpCAM+Vim+CD24- cells.

claim: OSCC are one of the top ten cancers worldwide, with over 300,000 cases annually.
source: OSCC are an important health burden and one of the top ten cancers worldwide, with over 300,000 cases annually and a 50% 5-year survival rate.
evidence: Statement of epidemiological facts.

claim: OSCC have a 50% 5-year survival rate.
source: OSCC are an important health burden and one of the top ten cancers worldwide, with over 300,000 cases annually and a 50% 5-year survival rate.
evidence: Statement of clinical outcome data.

claim: There is frequent metastatic spread of OSCC to the lymph nodes of the neck.
source: There is frequent metastatic spread to the lymph nodes of the neck; this is the single most important predictor of outcome and an important factor in treatment decisions (Sano and Myers, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior clinical literature.

claim: Lymph node metastasis is the single most important predictor of outcome in OSCC.
source: There is frequent metastatic spread to the lymph nodes of the neck; this is the single most important predictor of outcome and an important factor in treatment decisions (Sano and Myers, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior clinical literature.

claim: At presentation it is currently very difficult to determine which OSCC tumours are metastatic.
source: At presentation it is currently very difficult to determine which tumours are metastatic and this results in sub-optimal tailoring of treatment decisions.
evidence: Statement about current clinical limitations.

claim: Difficulty in determining metastatic status results in sub-optimal tailoring of treatment decisions for OSCC.
source: At presentation it is currently very difficult to determine which tumours are metastatic and this results in sub-optimal tailoring of treatment decisions.
evidence: Logical inference from the inability to accurately predict metastasis.

claim: Accurate prediction of metastasis would have great potential to improve clinical management of OSCC to reduce both mortality and treatment-related morbidity.
source: Accurate prediction of metastasis would therefore have great potential to improve clinical management of the disease to reduce both mortality and treatment-related morbidity.
evidence: Logical inference about the clinical utility of improved prediction.

claim: The best performing classifiers for EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 were the artificial neural network (ANN) and support vector machine (SVM), with F1 accuracy scores of 91% and 87% respectively.
source: The best performing classifiers for EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 were the artificial neural network (ANN) and support vector machine (SVM), with F1 accuracy scores of 91% and 87% respectfully (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by machine learning results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For the ANN trained on EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24, the area under the curve (AUC) accuracy score was 87%, with 94% sensitivity and 82% specificity.
source: For the ANN, the area under the curve (AUC) accuracy score was 87%, with 94% sensitivity and 82% specificity.
evidence: Supported by machine learning results.

claim: Training with Pan-keratin, Vimentin and CD24 gave much worse prediction across all classifiers compared to EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24.
source: Training with Pan-keratin, Vimentin and CD24 gave much worse prediction across all classifiers (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by machine learning results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Staining for EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 can predict metastatic status with high accuracy using a machine learning algorithm.
source: These findings demonstrate that, utilising a machine learning algorithm, staining for EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 can predict metastatic status with high accuracy and may therefore have clinical utility.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the machine learning results.

claim: EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 staining may have clinical utility for predicting metastasis.
source: These findings demonstrate that, utilising a machine learning algorithm, staining for EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 can predict metastatic status with high accuracy and may therefore have clinical utility.
evidence: Speculative statement about potential clinical application.

claim: The ANN trained using the first 24 specimens correctly predicted metastatic status for 54/59 slides in a blinded test of the second cohort.
source: Taking the majority prediction from the 10 fields of view from each slide, the ANN correctly predicted metastatic status for 54/59 slides (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by blinded validation results.

claim: An ANN trained on the second cohort achieved 89% accuracy after 12 training epochs.
source: For this task, we recorded the predictive accuracy from the training and validation sets after each training round ('epoch'), which showed good alignment and an 89% accuracy score after 12 training epochs (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by machine learning results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Feeding more imaging data into the ANN may only improve prediction up to a point.
source: Interestingly, this is a similar accuracy to the previous ANN trained using 3500 imaging fields from 24 specimens, suggesting that feeding more imaging data into the ANN may only improve prediction up to a point.
evidence: Inference from comparing the accuracy of ANNs trained on different amounts of data.

claim: Only the ANN trained using image pixel intensity values has predictive utility, not ANNs trained using summary cell count data.
source: The resulting ROC curves (Figure 3E) demonstrate that only the ANN trained using image pixel intensity values has predictive utility in our cohort.
evidence: Supported by comparison of ROC curves shown in Figure 3E.

claim: This is the first time immunofluorescent staining of human tumour tissue specimens has been used in a machine learning pipeline for clinical prediction.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first time immunofluorescent staining of human tumour tissue specimens has been used in a machine learning pipeline for clinical prediction.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the approach based on literature knowledge.

claim: Previous studies using cytokeratin immunohistochemistry, clinicopathological data and serum biomarkers for clinical prediction via machine learning have achieved AUCs of 75% in breast cancer.
source: Previous studies using cytokeratin immunohistochemistry, clinicopathological data and serum biomarkers for clinical prediction via machine learning have achieved AUCs of 75% in breast cancer (Tseng et al., 2019), 80% in OSCC (Bur et al., 2019), and 82% in colorectal cancer (Takamatsu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Previous studies using cytokeratin immunohistochemistry, clinicopathological data and serum biomarkers for clinical prediction via machine learning have achieved AUCs of 80% in OSCC.
source: Previous studies using cytokeratin immunohistochemistry, clinicopathological data and serum biomarkers for clinical prediction via machine learning have achieved AUCs of 75% in breast cancer (Tseng et al., 2019), 80% in OSCC (Bur et al., 2019), and 82% in colorectal cancer (Takamatsu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Previous studies using cytokeratin immunohistochemistry, clinicopathological data and serum biomarkers for clinical prediction via machine learning have achieved AUCs of 82% in colorectal cancer.
source: Previous studies using cytokeratin immunohistochemistry, clinicopathological data and serum biomarkers for clinical prediction via machine learning have achieved AUCs of 75% in breast cancer (Tseng et al., 2019), 80% in OSCC (Bur et al., 2019), and 82% in colorectal cancer (Takamatsu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The role of EMT in tumour dissemination has long been debated.
source: The role of EMT in tumour dissemination has long been debated but, lacking evidence of cells undergoing EMT whilst disseminating from human tumours in vivo, this role has had to be inferred from mouse models and human cell line models.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field.

claim: Lacking evidence of cells undergoing EMT whilst disseminating from human tumours in vivo, the role of EMT has had to be inferred from mouse models and human cell line models.
source: The role of EMT in tumour dissemination has long been debated but, lacking evidence of cells undergoing EMT whilst disseminating from human tumours in vivo, this role has had to be inferred from mouse models and human cell line models.
evidence: Statement about the limitations of prior evidence.

claim: Through applying understanding of EMT cancer cell heterogeneity and markers for EMT CSCs, EMT CSCs disseminating from the primary tumour in human pathological specimens have been identified.
source: Here, through applying our understanding of EMT cancer cell heterogeneity and markers for EMT CSCs, we have identified EMT CSCs disseminating from the primary tumour in human pathological specimens.
evidence: Summary of the study's main finding.

claim: The presence of disseminating EMT CSCs is strongly correlated with tumour metastasis.
source: Importantly, the presence of these disseminating stem cells is strongly correlated with tumour metastasis.
evidence: Supported by the quantification and machine learning results.

claim: A partial EMT state has previously been identified in an OSCC scRNAseq dataset.
source: A partial EMT state has previously been identified in an OSCC scRNAseq dataset; this state retained epithelial gene expression alongside expression of mesenchymal genes, and was correlated with nodal metastasis and adverse pathological features (Puram et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The partial EMT state identified in scRNAseq retained epithelial gene expression alongside expression of mesenchymal genes.
source: A partial EMT state has previously been identified in an OSCC scRNAseq dataset; this state retained epithelial gene expression alongside expression of mesenchymal genes, and was correlated with nodal metastasis and adverse pathological features (Puram et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The partial EMT state identified in scRNAseq was correlated with nodal metastasis and adverse pathological features.
source: A partial EMT state has previously been identified in an OSCC scRNAseq dataset; this state retained epithelial gene expression alongside expression of mesenchymal genes, and was correlated with nodal metastasis and adverse pathological features (Puram et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Epithelial keratins are not retained in disseminating EMT CSCs.
source: However, epithelial keratins are not retained.
evidence: Supported by the pan-keratin staining results.

claim: Retention of EpCAM is not on its own sufficient alongside Vimentin to mark disseminating EMT CSCs that correlate with metastasis.
source: We have also shown that retention of EpCAM is not on its own sufficient alongside Vimentin to mark disseminating EMT CSCs that correlate with metastasis.
evidence: Supported by the finding that EpCAM+Vim+CD24- cells do not correlate with metastasis.

claim: There is a requirement for CD24 to mark disseminating EMT CSCs that correlate with metastasis.
source: There is a requirement for CD24, which we have previously shown to be a plasticity marker within the EMT population even when driven into full morphological EMT under TGFβ treatment (Biddle et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by the differential correlation with metastasis and prior characterization of CD24.

claim: CD24 is a plasticity marker within the EMT population even when driven into full morphological EMT under TGFβ treatment.
source: There is a requirement for CD24, which we have previously shown to be a plasticity marker within the EMT population even when driven into full morphological EMT under TGFβ treatment (Biddle et al., 2016).
evidence: Refers to prior work by the authors.

claim: The EMT CSC state may be more complex than a simple coalescence of epithelial and mesenchymal characteristics.
source: This suggests that the EMT CSC state may be more complex than a simple coalescence of epithelial and mesenchymal characteristics.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the requirement for CD24 beyond just epithelial and mesenchymal markers.

claim: Image-based machine learning approaches employ a greater range of inputs to develop their predictions and often achieve greater predictive accuracy than machine learning approaches that use simpler data inputs.
source: Image-based machine learning approaches employ a greater range of inputs to develop their predictions, and therefore often achieve greater predictive accuracy than machine learning approaches that use simpler data inputs.
evidence: General statement about machine learning methodology.

claim: Image-based machine learning comes at the cost of increased computing requirements and reduced ability to decode the learning process.
source: This comes at the cost of increased computing requirements and reduced ability to decode the learning process (the so-called 'black box'), but in our study the image-based approach proved essential to achieve high predictive accuracy.
evidence: General statement about machine learning methodology and observation from the study.

claim: In this study, the image-based approach proved essential to achieve high predictive accuracy.
source: This comes at the cost of increased computing requirements and reduced ability to decode the learning process (the so-called 'black box'), but in our study the image-based approach proved essential to achieve high predictive accuracy.
evidence: Supported by the comparison of image-based vs summary data-based ANNs.

claim: The lack of improvement in predictive accuracy when trained on 9000 images compared to 3500 suggests a limitation of the ANN.
source: The lack of improvement in predictive accuracy when trained on a collection of 9000 images compared to 3500 suggests a limitation of the ANN, and a possible role for more sophisticated neural network architectures such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
evidence: Inference from the similar accuracy achieved with different amounts of training data.

claim: There is a possible role for more sophisticated neural network architectures such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to improve prediction.
source: The lack of improvement in predictive accuracy when trained on a collection of 9000 images compared to 3500 suggests a limitation of the ANN, and a possible role for more sophisticated neural network architectures such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
evidence: Speculative suggestion for future improvement.

claim: CNNs use the raw image for training, whereas ANNs are trained using intensity values for each pixel.
source: Whereas the ANN is trained using intensity values for each pixel, a CNN uses the raw image for training.
evidence: Statement about differences in machine learning architectures.

claim: CNNs require many more images for training but can reach higher levels of accuracy.
source: CNNs require many more images for training, but can reach higher levels of accuracy.
evidence: General statement about CNN characteristics.

claim: A further blinded cohort and a greater number of tumour specimens would be valuable to support the conclusions of this study.
source: To support the conclusions of this study, a further blinded cohort and a greater number of tumour specimens would be valuable.
evidence: Statement about future validation needs.

claim: Immunofluorescent antibody co-staining for EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 can separate disseminating EMT CSCs from the stromal content of human tumours.
source: We have shown that immunofluorescent antibody co-staining for EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 can separate disseminating EMT CSCs from the stromal content of human tumours, a challenge which has confounded previous attempts to develop a predictive EMT signature (Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by the imaging and quantification results.

claim: Previous attempts to develop a predictive EMT signature have been confounded by the challenge of separating EMT cells from stromal content.
source: We have shown that immunofluorescent antibody co-staining for EpCAM, Vimentin and CD24 can separate disseminating EMT CSCs from the stromal content of human tumours, a challenge which has confounded previous attempts to develop a predictive EMT signature (Tan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work.

claim: EpCAM+Vim+CD24- tumour cells in the stroma do not correlate with metastasis.
source: We also show that EpCAM+Vim+CD24- tumour cells in the stroma do not correlate with metastasis, and therefore the clinically predictive utility of tumour cell staining in the stroma can be isolated specifically to the EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ EMT CSCs.
evidence: Supported by quantification data.

claim: The clinically predictive utility of tumour cell staining in the stroma can be isolated specifically to the EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ EMT CSCs.
source: We also show that EpCAM+Vim+CD24- tumour cells in the stroma do not correlate with metastasis, and therefore the clinically predictive utility of tumour cell staining in the stroma can be isolated specifically to the EpCAM+Vim+CD24+ EMT CSCs.
evidence: Inference from the differential correlation with metastasis.

claim: Using techniques that give single cell resolution enables isolation of the signal to the specific cell type of interest within a highly heterogeneous cellular environment.
